The method concerns the control of non-productive movement of a machine tool, such as a rapid traverse movement, from a starting position to an end position within a defined travel envelope. The travel envelope represents the spatial region in which the machine tool, or a movable component of the machine tool, is permitted to move.

To carry out the movement safely, a first trajectory is initially provided. This first trajectory defines a collision-free path from the starting position to the end position. In particular, the first trajectory may be composed of a plurality of rectilinear segments, so that the machine tool reaches the end position by following a sequence of straight-line movements while avoiding obstacles within the travel envelope.

An algorithm is then used to determine a second trajectory for the same non-productive movement. The second trajectory is generated so as to improve upon the first trajectory with respect to at least one selectable target parameter. The target parameter may be, for example, movement time, path length, energy consumption, smoothness of motion, mechanical loading, or another optimization criterion relevant to operation of the machine tool.

Unlike the first trajectory, which includes multiple rectilinear segments, the second trajectory includes at least one polynomial segment. The use of a polynomial segment allows the movement to be shaped more smoothly and may reduce abrupt changes in direction, acceleration, or jerk. As a result, the second trajectory can provide a more efficient or mechanically favorable movement while still connecting the starting position and the end position.

After the second trajectory has been determined, it is checked for collisions within the travel envelope. If the second trajectory is collision-free, it may be used to control the non-productive movement of the machine tool. If, however, the second trajectory is found not to be collision-free, the algorithm is repeated. In that case, the model of the travel envelope used by the algorithm is modified, for example by adding, enlarging, or otherwise adapting restricted regions corresponding to potential collisions. The repeated algorithm then determines a further trajectory on the basis of the modified model, with the aim of obtaining an improved trajectory that is also free of collisions.

A method is provided for controlling non-productive tool movement in a machine tool, particularly movement that occurs between machining operations and does not itself remove material from a workpiece. The method begins by determining an initial travel path for the tool or tool carrier. This initial path is a rectilinear trajectory, meaning that it is composed of straight-line movement sections, and is selected so that it is free from collisions with the workpiece, fixtures, machine components, or other obstacles in the working space of the machine tool.

Starting from this collision-free rectilinear trajectory, an optimization process is then carried out. The optimization process uses an algorithm to convert or transform the initial trajectory into an improved polynomial trajectory. The polynomial trajectory may include curved or smoothly blended movement sections rather than only straight-line segments. The optimization is performed with respect to at least one selectable target parameter. This target parameter may be, for example, a reduction in travel time, a reduction in path length, a limitation of acceleration or jerk, an improvement in energy efficiency, smoother axis movement, or a combination of such criteria.

After the optimized polynomial trajectory has been generated, it is checked for possible collisions. This collision check may be performed using a model of the machine tool environment, including the tool, tool holder, spindle, workpiece, clamping devices, and any other relevant objects or exclusion zones. If the collision check determines that the polynomial trajectory is collision-free, the optimized trajectory is accepted. It is then used as the movement instruction for the machine tool to carry out the non-productive movement.

If, however, the collision check identifies a potential collision, the optimized trajectory is not accepted in its current form. Instead, the optimization is repeated. For the repeated optimization, a travel-envelope model used by the algorithm is modified. The travel-envelope model defines the permissible spatial region or movement corridor within which the tool or machine component is allowed to move. By modifying this model, the algorithm is guided away from areas that caused or could cause collisions and is encouraged to produce a new trajectory that remains within safer regions of the workspace.

This iterative procedure may be repeated until a polynomial trajectory is found that satisfies the selected optimization target while also being free from collisions. In this way, the method combines the reliability of an initially collision-free rectilinear movement path with the efficiency advantages of optimized, smooth polynomial motion. The result is a safer and more efficient control strategy for non-productive movements of a machine tool, reducing unnecessary travel time while maintaining collision protection.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest and most common words in the English language, yet it plays an important role in communication. It is called a definite article, and it helps identify something specific. For example, when we say “a book,” we could mean any book, but when we say “the book,” we are talking about a particular one.

This simple word adds clarity and precision to sentences. It guides the reader or listener toward a known person, place, object, or idea. Without “the,” many sentences would feel incomplete or unclear.

Although “the” may seem ordinary, it is essential in everyday speech and writing. It proves that even the smallest words can have great importance in language.

1. **A method of controlling a machine tool during non-cutting motion**, the method comprising:  
   moving, by a controller of the machine tool, a tool from a start point toward an end point along an initial rectilinear path determined to be collision-safe;  
   generating, by the controller, a candidate non-rectilinear path between the start point and the end point, the candidate non-rectilinear path being represented by a polynomial function;  
   evaluating the candidate non-rectilinear path for collision with at least one obstacle within a machine workspace using an envelope model associated with at least one of the tool, a tool holder, a spindle, a workpiece, or a machine component;  
   when the candidate non-rectilinear path is determined to be collision-free, commanding the machine tool to execute the candidate non-rectilinear path during the non-cutting motion; and  
   when the candidate non-rectilinear path is determined to collide with the at least one obstacle, adjusting the envelope model and repeating the generating and evaluating steps using the adjusted envelope model until a collision-free polynomial path is obtained.

2. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the initial rectilinear path comprises at least one straight-line segment displaced from the at least one obstacle by a predetermined safety clearance.

3. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the polynomial function comprises a spline, a Bézier curve, a B-spline, or a higher-order polynomial trajectory.

4. **The method of claim 1**, wherein generating the candidate non-rectilinear path comprises optimizing at least one of travel time, path length, acceleration, jerk, axis motion, or clearance from the at least one obstacle.

5. **The method of claim 1**, wherein adjusting the envelope model comprises expanding, shrinking, offsetting, reshaping, or otherwise modifying a swept volume used for collision detection.

6. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the envelope model defines a swept volume of the tool or tool assembly along the candidate non-rectilinear path.

7. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the non-cutting motion comprises rapid traverse motion of the machine tool.

8. **The method of claim 1**, wherein the controller stores the initial rectilinear path as a fallback path and executes the initial rectilinear path if no collision-free polynomial path is obtained within a predetermined number of iterations or computation time.

9. **A machine tool control system**, comprising:  
   one or more processors; and  
   memory storing instructions that, when executed by the one or more processors, cause the control system to:  
   determine a collision-safe rectilinear path for moving a tool from a start point to an end point during non-cutting motion;  
   compute a candidate polynomial path between the start point and the end point;  
   perform collision checking of the candidate polynomial path using an envelope model of at least a portion of the machine tool or a workpiece environment;  
   in response to detecting no collision, output motion commands causing the machine tool to move the tool along the candidate polynomial path; and  
   in response to detecting a collision, modify the envelope model and iteratively compute and collision-check a further candidate polynomial path until a collision-free polynomial path is identified.

10. **A non-transitory computer-readable medium** storing instructions that, when executed by a controller of a machine tool, cause the controller to perform the method of claim 1.
